all_historical_figures.name: Āgama
all_historical_figures.significance: Credited with the 'convention of mudrās' as a contribution to Indian culture.

all_historical_figures.name: Hanumān
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the context of delivering Rāma's signet-ring (mudrikā) to Sītā.

all_historical_figures.name: Sītā
all_historical_figures.significance: Recipient of Rāma's signet-ring from Hanumān.

all_historical_figures.name: Rāma
all_historical_figures.significance: His signet-ring is used as a token of identity.

all_historical_figures.name: Kālidāsa
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned for using the idea of a recovered signet-ring as a key plot device in his play Abhijñāna-Śakuntalam.

all_historical_figures.name: Duṣyanta
all_historical_figures.significance: His lost and recovered signet-ring drives the plot's resolution.

all_historical_figures.name: Nātha-siddhas
all_historical_figures.significance: The expression 'mudrā' was widely used in their mystic cults.

all_historical_figures.name: Buddha
all_historical_figures.significance: The stylization of his iconography in sculpture led to the frequent use of mudrās to represent his actions and divine nature.

all_historical_figures.name: Bharata
all_historical_figures.significance: His text on dramaturgy is a key source for the study of mudrās (hastas) in dance and drama.

all_historical_figures.name: Nandikeśvara
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the Abhinaya-darpaṇa, a text that enumerates and describes 115 hand-poses.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: Central deity in the Vaiṣṇava division of Āgama, associated with numerous mudrās, including the practice of branding with his weapon symbols.

all_historical_figures.name: Gautama
all_historical_figures.significance: His Mudrā-dhāraṇa-vidhi is cited for prescribing the wearing of Viṣṇu's emblems on the body.

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: The highest deity in Śaivāgama, whose energies (śaktis) are said to be the mudrās themselves. Numerous mudrās are associated with his worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Bhaṭṭa-nārāyaṇa-kaṇṭha
all_historical_figures.significance: Commentator on the Mṛgendrāgama, interpreting 'mudrā' as a subjugating force of the highest deity.

all_historical_figures.name: Siddhakarṇa-Pa
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing mahārāja-līlā pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Siddha Siṃha-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated holding an akṣa-mālā.

all_historical_figures.name: Siddhāchāryā-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in utthita-pāda pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Siddha Avadhūti-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in vismaya and kapāla pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Vajra-Pāṇi
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in a specific pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Saraha-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in a specific pose.

all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in a specific pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Śabari-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in a specific pose, including one with a bow and arrow (dhanur-bāṇa-mudrā).

all_historical_figures.name: Jālandhara Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing dhyāna-mudrā and dharma-cakra-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Kṛṣṇa-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing dhyāna-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Gsang-Ba-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing viśva-vajra-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vijaya-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing vedha-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Sgam-Po-Pa
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing samādhi-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Milarepa
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing divya-dhvani mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vajra-Sattva

all_historical_figures.name: Vajra-Dharma
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing praṇidhāna-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vimalamitra
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated in a specific pose.

all_historical_figures.name: Padma-Sambhava
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing guru-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vairocana
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing vyākhyāna-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Śānto-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing akṣa-mālā-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Tantra-Pāda
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing dīkṣā-mudrā.

all_historical_figures.name: Vīṇā-Dhara
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing vīṇa-vādana-mudrā (playing the vīṇa).

all_historical_figures.name: Kāma
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing dhanur-bāṇa-mudrā (holding bow and arrow).

all_historical_figures.name: Kurukullā
all_historical_figures.significance: Illustrated performing gestures with dhanur-bāṇa-kapāla and aṅkuśa.

all_historical_figures.name: Indra
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in the Mahābhārata as the divine overseer of the hands, highlighting their spiritual importance.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.significance: The sacred waters of Brahmā are said to reside at the base of the thumb. A myth involving Śiva cutting off one of his heads is used to explain the name of the ring-finger ('anāmikā').

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Mentioned in a myth where he cuts off one of Brahmā's heads with his ring-finger, rendering the finger 'nameless' ('anāmikā'). The 'liṅga-mudrā' is specific to his worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: In Vaiṣṇava worship, the five finger-manipulations in mānasa-pūjā represent his five forms: Nārāyaṇa, Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. The 'śaṁkha-mudrā' is specific to his worship.

all_historical_figures.name: Nandikeśvara
all_historical_figures.significance: Quoted for his explanation of the purpose of hand-poses in dance, which is used to illustrate the principle of how mudrās focus attention and evoke emotion.

all_historical_figures.name: Bharata-muni
all_historical_figures.significance: His codification of hand gestures (hastas) in the Nāṭya-śāstra is cited as being directly relevant to the mudrās used in worship, particularly his division of 'samyuta-hastas' (two-handed gestures).
all_historical_figures.dates: Traditionally dated between 200 BCE and 200 CE

all_historical_figures.name: Bharata
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the 'Natyā-śāstra', which prescribes the 'pūrva-raṅga' preliminary sequence for stage shows.

all_historical_figures.name: Nandikeśvara
all_historical_figures.significance: Author of the 'Abhinaya-darpaṇa', which contains sections on mudrās specific to divinities.

all_historical_figures.name: Viśva-karmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Regarded as the first architect of the theatre in the context of the 'pūrva-raṅga'.

all_historical_figures.name: Mitra
all_historical_figures.significance: The presiding deity of the green-room (nepathya).

all_historical_figures.name: Varuṇa
all_historical_figures.significance: Presided over the upper realms of the theatre; also one of the Dikpālas (guardian of the West).

all_historical_figures.name: Agni
all_historical_figures.significance: Was in charge of the theatre itself; also one of the Dikpālas (guardian of the South-East).

all_historical_figures.name: Megha
all_historical_figures.significance: Guarded the musical instruments.

all_historical_figures.name: Brahmā
all_historical_figures.significance: Protected the platform; one of the Dikpālas (guardian of the realm above).

all_historical_figures.name: Indra
all_historical_figures.significance: Protected the chief actor-dancer (nāyaka); one of the Dikpālas (guardian of the East).

all_historical_figures.name: Sarasvati
all_historical_figures.significance: Protected the female counterpart of the chief actor-dancer (nāyaki).

all_historical_figures.name: Śiva
all_historical_figures.significance: Protected the other participants of the dance-drama.

all_historical_figures.name: Viṣṇu
all_historical_figures.significance: Major deity for whom nineteen specific mudrās are described.

all_historical_figures.name: Gaṇeśa (Gaṇapati)
all_historical_figures.significance: Deity for whom seven specific mudrās are described.

all_historical_figures.name: Pārvati
all_historical_figures.significance: A major goddess for whom specific mudrās are listed.

all_historical_figures.name: Lakṣmī
all_historical_figures.significance: A major goddess for whom specific mudrās are listed.

all_historical_figures.name: Tārā
all_historical_figures.significance: A tantrik deity for whom five specific mudrās are described.

all_historical_figures.name: Tripurā
all_historical_figures.significance: The special form of the mother-goddess worshipped in Śrī-cakra, for whom ten mudrās are described.

complete_timeline.event: Creation and protection of the first theatre
complete_timeline.significance: Described as part of the 'pūrva-raṅga' tradition from the Natyā-śāstra, it establishes the divine sanction and protection for the performance arts, with various deities assigned specific roles.

complete_timeline.date: Not specified, but historically c. 1st century BCE - 1st century CE
complete_timeline.significance: Led to an emphasized aspect of Mudrā, associating hand-gestures with mantras and mandalas in tantric contexts to reinforce occult power.

complete_timeline.event: Development of stylized Buddha iconography with mudrās
complete_timeline.date: as early as the third or second century after Christ (CE)
complete_timeline.significance: Marks the period when the use of mudrās in sculpture became frequent, particularly in the Gandhara and Mathura schools, to represent the Buddha in human form and convey his divine personality and actions.

all_geographic_locations.context: Located 'in the northwestern corner of the country', it was a major center for the stylization of Buddha iconography and the use of mudrās in sculpture.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A key site for the historical development of mudrās in art.

all_geographic_locations.context: Located 'on the banks of the river Yamunā', it is described as the place where Indian iconography appears to have evolved, with the Buddha beginning to be represented in human form with mudrās.
all_geographic_locations.significance: A foundational site for the development of Indian and Buddhist iconography.

all_geographic_locations.context: The primary cultural and geographical origin of the mudrā tradition.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Homeland of Āgama, Tantra, and the traditions discussed.

all_geographic_locations.place: Nepāl, Tibet, Mongolia, China and Japan
all_geographic_locations.context: Countries where Buddhist versions of Tantra, which extensively use mudrās, prevail.
all_geographic_locations.significance: Shows the geographical spread and influence of the mudrā tradition beyond India.
